position: before its word — usually a past participle (*ornately carved*)

senses.gloss: With a lot of detailed decoration.
examples: The ceiling was *ornately* painted with angels and clouds.
She wore an *ornately* embroidered silk jacket.
The old theater's lobby is *ornately* decorated in red and gold.

type: stance — what is claimed, which may not be the real reason
position: mid — or before the phrase it comments on; also front
modifies: clauses and phrases, especially reasons (*ostensibly to…*)

senses.gloss: As it appears or is said to be, though perhaps not really.
examples: He left the meeting early, *ostensibly* to catch a flight.
The trip was *ostensibly* about trade, but everyone knew it was political.
*Ostensibly*, the new rule is meant to protect customers.

senses.gloss: In a showy way meant to attract attention or impress people.
examples: He *ostentatiously* checked his gold watch.
Their house is *ostentatiously* decorated, with marble everywhere.
She yawned *ostentatiously* while he was talking.

position: before its word — usually an adjective or participle (*outlandishly dressed*)

senses.gloss: In a very strange or unusual way, often to a ridiculous degree.
examples: He showed up *outlandishly* dressed in a purple cape.
The prices at that resort are *outlandishly* high.
She decorated her apartment *outlandishly*, with neon signs on every wall.

position: before its word — or end when it describes behavior

senses.gloss: Extremely, to a shocking degree — often about prices, cost or humor.
examples: Rents in this neighborhood are *outrageously* expensive.
The movie was *outrageously* funny.
Concert tickets have gotten *outrageously* overpriced.

senses.gloss: In a shocking or offensive way.
examples: The fans behaved *outrageously* after the game.
He flirted *outrageously* with everyone at the party.

type: manner — openly, completely, or at once
position: end — after the verb or its object
contrast: The adjective goes before a noun and is stressed on the first syllable: *an outright lie* (ˈaʊtraɪt), *an outright ban*. The adverb comes after the verb: *They banned it outright*.

senses.gloss: Openly and completely, without holding anything back.
examples: The board rejected the plan *outright*.
She didn't lie *outright*, but she left out a lot.
He asked me *outright* whether I was quitting.

senses.gloss: Fully and at once, not in parts or over time.
examples: They bought the house *outright*, with no mortgage.
Two passengers were killed *outright* in the crash.

senses.gloss: Extremely well or to an extremely high degree; far better than usual.
examples: The team played *outstandingly* well this season.
She was an *outstandingly* talented pianist.
The new vaccine has been *outstandingly* successful.

type: stance — how things look, as opposed to how they are
modifies: adjectives (*outwardly calm*), verbs and whole clauses
contrast: For direction (наружу) use *outward*: *The door opens outward*. *Outwardly* is about appearance: *outwardly calm* = внешне спокойный.

senses.gloss: On the surface; in the way someone or something appears.
senses.ru: внешне, с виду, на первый взгляд
examples: She stayed *outwardly* calm, but her hands were shaking.
*Outwardly*, the two brothers seemed to get along.
The building looks *outwardly* the same, but the inside is brand new.

contrast: *Overly* is especially common in American English; British English often uses the prefix instead (*over-cautious*). *Not overly* is a polite understatement: *I'm not overly worried* = я не особенно волнуюсь.

senses.gloss: Too; more than is reasonable or necessary.
examples: Don't be *overly* critical of yourself.
The instructions were *overly* complicated.
I'm not *overly* worried about the test.

type: degree — so strongly that it is hard to bear
position: before its word — or after a verb like *smell*

senses.gloss: So strongly that it overwhelms you.
examples: The room smelled *overpoweringly* of cheap perfume.
The sauce was *overpoweringly* salty.
It was *overpoweringly* hot inside the car.

type: duration — beyond the regular working hours
contrast: Also a noun: *get paid overtime* (сверхурочные), *The game went into overtime* (дополнительное время). *Work overtime* is the adverb, and *working overtime* is also used figuratively for something very busy.

senses.gloss: Beyond the usual hours of work.
examples: The nurses worked *overtime* all week.
He's been working *overtime* to pay off his student loans.
Her imagination was working *overtime* after the scary movie.

senses.gloss: Openly, in a way that is not hidden.
examples: The ad isn't *overtly* political, but the message is clear.
He never *overtly* threatened anyone.
Some voters were *overtly* hostile to the idea.

position: before its word — or end (*passed overwhelmingly*)

senses.gloss: To a very great degree; by a very large majority.
examples: The bill passed *overwhelmingly*.
Voters are *overwhelmingly* in favor of the new park.
The reviews have been *overwhelmingly* positive.

type: time — after noon, with a clock time
position: after its word — after the number
form: abbreviation of Latin *post meridiem*, after noon
contrast: Americans use the 12-hour clock where Russian uses 19:00: say *7 p.m.* Use it only after a number: not *in the p.m.*, not *7 o'clock p.m.*, and not *7 p.m. in the evening* (the evening is already in *p.m.*). *12 p.m.* is noon, which confuses people, so say *noon* or *midnight*.

senses.gloss: After noon — used after a time between noon and midnight.
examples: The store closes at 9 *p.m.*
My flight lands at 6:45 *p.m.* Eastern time.
Office hours are 1 to 4 *p.m.*, Monday through Friday.

position: before its word — or end when it means with pain

senses.gloss: Very, to an unpleasant degree — often with *slow*, *shy*, *aware* or *obvious*.
examples: The line at the DMV moved *painfully* slowly.
She was *painfully* shy as a child.
It was *painfully* obvious that he hadn't read the book.

senses.gloss: In a way that causes physical or emotional pain.
examples: He fell *painfully* on his elbow.
Her knee was still *painfully* swollen.

senses.gloss: Without pain, or without trouble or difficulty.
examples: The tooth came out quickly and *painlessly*.
The switch to the new software went *painlessly*.
You can renew your license *painlessly* online.

position: mid or end — also before a participle (*painstakingly restored*)

senses.gloss: With great care and attention to every detail.
examples: The old car was *painstakingly* restored.
She *painstakingly* checked every number in the report.
They rebuilt the bridge *painstakingly*, stone by stone.

type: degree — so strongly it can almost be felt

senses.gloss: So clearly that it can almost be touched or felt.
examples: The crowd was *palpably* nervous before the final shot.
The claim is *palpably* false.
The mood in the office has *palpably* changed since the layoffs.

type: stance — the opposite of what you would expect

senses.gloss: In a way that seems to contradict itself or what you would expect.
examples: *Paradoxically*, the more choices people have, the less happy they feel.
The drug is *paradoxically* more effective at lower doses.
The quietest kid in class was, *paradoxically*, the best public speaker.

modifies: verbs of saying and whole clauses

senses.gloss: As an extra remark, added in passing.
examples: She mentioned, almost *parenthetically*, that she was moving to Chicago.
*Parenthetically*, I should add that the data is from 2019.
The author notes *parenthetically* that the study was never repeated.

position: before its word — usually in pairs (*part …, part …*)
contrast: *Part* is usually a noun (*a part of the plan*). As an adverb it comes before a noun or adjective, most often in pairs: *part man, part wolf*. Before a single adjective, *partly* sounds more natural: *partly true*.

senses.gloss: Partly; to some extent — often in pairs.
examples: The creature was *part* man, *part* wolf.
The trip was *part* business, *part* vacation.
Her dog is *part* husky.

type: duration — for only part of the usual working hours
contrast: Adverb after a verb: *She works part-time*. Adjective before a noun: *a part-time job*. The opposite is *full-time*.

senses.gloss: For only part of the normal working or study hours.
examples: She works *part-time* at a bookstore.
He's studying *part-time* while he raises two kids.
Many students work *part-time* to pay for college.

type: degree — well enough, but not very well

senses.gloss: Fairly; well enough to be acceptable.
examples: He speaks *passably* good Spanish.
The food was *passably* decent for an airport.
She plays the guitar *passably* well.

senses.gloss: With strong feeling or great enthusiasm.
examples: She spoke *passionately* about climate change.
They kissed *passionately* at the airport.
He believes *passionately* that everyone deserves a second chance.

senses.gloss: Without taking action or resisting; just accepting what happens.
examples: Don't just sit *passively* and wait for things to change.
Most people watch TV *passively*.
She *passively* accepted whatever her boss said.

type: manner — only in *down pat* and *stand pat*
modifies: *down* in *have something down pat*, and *stand* in *stand pat*
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *pat*
contrast: The adjective before a noun is critical: *a pat answer* is a quick, rehearsed reply (шаблонный, заученный ответ). The verb and noun *pat* mean похлопать, похлопывание: *pat the dog*. *Stand pat* comes from poker and is mainly American.

senses.gloss: Perfectly, learned by heart — in *have* or *get something down pat*.
examples: She practiced her speech until she had it down *pat*.
It took me a month to get the dance steps down *pat*.

senses.gloss: Without changing anything — in *stand pat*, keep a decision or position.
examples: The Fed is expected to stand *pat* on interest rates this month.
Despite the losing streak, the team stood *pat* at the trade deadline.

type: degree — obviously, usually with a negative adjective

senses.gloss: Very clearly; in a way nobody can doubt.
examples: That claim is *patently* false.
It was *patently* obvious that she didn't want to go.
The rule is *patently* unfair to part-time workers.

contrast: False friend: *pathetically* is not патетически (with pathos, grandly). It means жалко or жалобно, and often shows contempt: *pathetically low pay*. For патетически use *with great emotion* or *grandly*.

senses.gloss: So badly or so little that it deserves pity or scorn.
examples: The pay is *pathetically* low.
Our team played *pathetically* in the second half.
He was *pathetically* grateful for any attention.

senses.gloss: In a sad way that makes people feel sorry for you.
examples: The puppy whimpered *pathetically* outside the door.
She looked up at me *pathetically* and asked for help.

type: degree — to an extreme, unhealthy degree

senses.gloss: To an extreme degree that seems like an illness.
examples: He's *pathologically* afraid of flying.
She's *pathologically* shy around strangers.
My boss is *pathologically* unable to admit a mistake.

senses.gloss: Calmly, without getting annoyed or in a hurry.
examples: We waited *patiently* for our turn.
She *patiently* explained the rules again.
The teacher listened *patiently* to every excuse.

position: mid or end — also before a participle (*patriotically decorated*)

senses.gloss: In a way that shows love for and loyalty to your country.
examples: The whole street was *patriotically* decorated for the Fourth of July.
They sang the anthem *patriotically*, hands on their hearts.
He *patriotically* joined the army after the attack.

senses.gloss: In a way that treats someone as less intelligent or important than you.
examples: He smiled *patronizingly* and said I'd understand when I was older.
Don't talk to me so *patronizingly*.
She *patronizingly* explained how to use a microwave.

contrast: *Peaceably* stresses behaving without fighting and sounds formal or legal (the First Amendment's *peaceably to assemble*). *Peacefully* is the everyday word and also means calmly, quietly: *sleeping peacefully*, never *sleeping peaceably*.

senses.gloss: Without fighting or causing trouble.
examples: The protesters gathered *peaceably* outside city hall.
The two sides settled the dispute *peaceably*.
The First Amendment protects the right of the people *peaceably* to assemble.

senses.gloss: Without violence or fighting.
examples: The protest ended *peacefully*.
The two countries resolved the conflict *peacefully*.

senses.gloss: Calmly and quietly.
examples: The baby was sleeping *peacefully* in her crib.
He died *peacefully* at home, surrounded by family.

senses.gloss: In a strange or unusual way.
examples: He's been acting *peculiarly* all week.
The streets were *peculiarly* quiet for a Saturday night.

senses.gloss: Especially; in a way typical of one person, place or group.
examples: It's a *peculiarly* American way of thinking about money.
The problem is *peculiarly* difficult for small towns.

type: viewpoint — from the point of view of teaching

senses.gloss: In terms of teaching and how people learn.
examples: The method is *pedagogically* sound but hard to use in large classes.
*Pedagogically*, it makes more sense to teach listening before grammar.
The textbook is *pedagogically* outdated.

contrast: Russian педантичный is often praise (аккуратный, пунктуальный). English *pedantic* and *pedantically* are criticism: too concerned with small rules and details, showing off knowledge. For praise use *meticulously* or *carefully*.

senses.gloss: In a way that is too concerned with small details or rules.
examples: "Technically, a tomato is a fruit," he said *pedantically*.
She *pedantically* corrected every comma in my email.
Don't be so *pedantically* literal about the rules.

type: manner — about how a word or name is used
modifies: verbs of using and naming (*use*, *call*, *refer to*)

senses.gloss: In a way that shows disapproval or a low opinion.
examples: The word "nerd" was once used only *pejoratively*.
Some people use "millennial" *pejoratively*.
She didn't mean "ambitious" *pejoratively*; it was a compliment.

senses.gloss: In a hurried, confused and disorderly way.
examples: The kids ran *pell-mell* out of the school when the bell rang.
Clothes were thrown *pell-mell* into the suitcase.
The crowd rushed *pell-mell* toward the exits.

senses.gloss: In a quiet, thoughtful way, often a little sad.
examples: She stared *pensively* out the window.
He stroked his beard *pensively*.
"I'm not sure," she said *pensively*.

contrast: Do not mix up *perceptibly* (noticeably, заметно) and *perceptively* (with insight, проницательно).

senses.gloss: Enough to be noticed.
examples: The temperature dropped *perceptibly* after sunset.
Her voice was *perceptibly* shaky.
Traffic hasn't improved *perceptibly* since the new lanes opened.

contrast: Do not mix up *perceptively* (with insight, проницательно) and *perceptibly* (noticeably, заметно).

senses.gloss: With a quick and deep understanding of people or situations.
examples: The critic writes *perceptively* about family relationships.
She *perceptively* noticed that something was wrong.
He commented *perceptively* on the weaknesses of the plan.

senses.gloss: In a sudden, commanding way that allows no discussion.
examples: The judge *peremptorily* dismissed the case.
She waved him away *peremptorily*.
He was *peremptorily* fired without any explanation.

ru: постоянно, вечно, из года в год

senses.gloss: Always, or again and again over many years.
senses.ru: постоянно, вечно, из года в год
examples: It's a *perennially* popular vacation spot.
Parking is a *perennially* sore subject in this town.
The team is *perennially* at the bottom of the league.

senses.gloss: Quickly and without real interest or care, only because you have to.
examples: The guard checked our IDs *perfunctorily* and waved us through.
She smiled *perfunctorily* and went back to her phone.
He *perfunctorily* apologized and changed the subject.

type: degree — dangerously, most often in *perilously close*

senses.gloss: Dangerously; in a way that could easily lead to disaster.
examples: The car stopped *perilously* close to the edge of the cliff.
The company came *perilously* close to bankruptcy.
The ladder leaned *perilously* against the wall.

type: degree — only slightly, at the edges

senses.gloss: Only in a minor way, not at the center of something.
examples: I was only *peripherally* involved in the project.
The book deals with the war only *peripherally*.
That issue is only *peripherally* related to what we're discussing.

senses.gloss: At a right angle to something, or straight up.
examples: The two streets run *perpendicularly* to each other.
Cut the board *perpendicularly* to the grain.
The cliff rises almost *perpendicularly* from the sea.

senses.gloss: All the time, or so often that it seems like all the time.
examples: My brother is *perpetually* late.
She seems *perpetually* tired these days.
The printer is *perpetually* out of ink.

senses.gloss: Again and again, refusing to give up.
examples: He *persistently* asked for a raise until they gave him one.
Reporters questioned her *persistently* about the scandal.

senses.gloss: For a long time, without stopping or improving.
examples: Unemployment has remained *persistently* high.
Children who are *persistently* absent fall behind.

senses.gloss: In a way that makes people believe or agree.
examples: She argued *persuasively* for a four-day workweek.
The article makes the case *persuasively*.
He writes clearly and *persuasively*.

ru: как ни странно; назло, из упрямства
position: mid — or front as a comment on the whole sentence
contrast: Usually not извращённо: *perversely* most often means against what you would expect or want. *Perversely, sales went up* = как ни странно, продажи выросли.

senses.gloss: Strangely, in a way that is the opposite of what you would expect.
examples: *Perversely*, the price went up as demand fell.
The long delay *perversely* made the fans even more excited.

senses.gloss: Deliberately doing the opposite of what is wanted or reasonable.
examples: She *perversely* turned down the job everyone told her to take.
He *perversely* enjoys arguing with people who agree with him.

senses.gloss: In a way that expects bad things to happen.
examples: Economists view the next quarter *pessimistically*.
"We'll never finish on time," he said *pessimistically*.
She *pessimistically* predicted that the repairs would take six months.

senses.gloss: In a bad-tempered, childish way, like someone who didn't get what they wanted.
examples: "I don't want to go," the boy said *petulantly*.
She *petulantly* slammed the door.
He tossed his phone *petulantly* onto the couch.

senses.gloss: Extremely; to an amazing degree.
examples: The app has been *phenomenally* successful.
She's a *phenomenally* talented singer.
The show did *phenomenally* well in its first season.

position: end — or front for the viewpoint sense

senses.gloss: Calmly, accepting something bad that cannot be changed.
examples: He took the news of the layoffs *philosophically*.
"Well, that's life," she said *philosophically*.

senses.gloss: From the point of view of philosophy.
examples: *Philosophically*, the two thinkers had a lot in common.
The question is *philosophically* interesting but hard to test.

senses.gloss: According to the sounds of speech, or the way a word is pronounced.
examples: Write the name *phonetically* so I know how to say it.
Young kids often spell words *phonetically*, like "nite" for "night."
The two words are *phonetically* identical but spelled differently.

type: viewpoint — in terms of how the body works

senses.gloss: In terms of how living bodies work.
examples: Fear and excitement are *physiologically* very similar.
*Physiologically*, the body can survive only a few days without water.
Babies are *physiologically* ready for solid food at about six months.

form: compound of *piece* and old *-meal*, by portions
contrast: Also an adjective before a noun, often critical: *a piecemeal approach* (бессистемный подход).

senses.gloss: A little at a time, not as a whole or according to a plan.
examples: The old house was renovated *piecemeal* over ten years.
Information came out *piecemeal*, one leak at a time.
Don't fix the problems *piecemeal*; we need a real plan.

contrast: Also a noun (*give me a piggyback*, *a piggyback ride*) and a verb meaning to use something that already exists: *piggyback on someone's idea*.

senses.gloss: On someone's back, with arms around their neck.
examples: The little girl rode *piggyback* on her dad.
He carried his son *piggyback* all the way home.
The kids took turns riding *piggyback*.

modifies: adjectives (*piercingly cold*, *piercingly blue*) and verbs of sound

senses.gloss: Sharply and intensely, as if cutting through something.
examples: She screamed *piercingly* when she saw the snake.
He had *piercingly* blue eyes.
The wind off the lake was *piercingly* cold.

senses.gloss: In a deeply religious way.
examples: The old woman prayed *piously* every morning.
They bowed their heads *piously* during the blessing.

senses.gloss: In a way that shows off how morally good you think you are.
examples: Politicians talk *piously* about family values.
He *piously* reminded us that he never drinks.

ru: обжигающе, с пылу с жару (только *piping hot*)
contrast: The adverb exists only in *piping hot*. Elsewhere *piping* is a noun (трубы; кант на одежде) or a form of the verb *pipe*.

senses.gloss: Very — used only in *piping hot*, about food or drink.
examples: The pizza came out of the oven *piping* hot.
Serve the soup *piping* hot.
Make sure the chicken is *piping* hot all the way through.

modifies: verbs of saying and writing (*put*, *sum up*, *write*)

senses.gloss: In a short, clever way that says a lot in few words.
examples: As one critic *pithily* put it, the movie is all trailer and no film.
She summed up the problem *pithily*: too many meetings, not enough work.
The review was *pithily* written and very funny.

senses.gloss: Sadly or shamefully too little — often with *small*, *few* or *low*.
examples: The pay was *pitifully* low.
*Pitifully* few people showed up to vote.

senses.gloss: In a way that makes people feel pity.
examples: The kitten mewed *pitifully* in the rain.
He limped *pitifully* back to the bench.

senses.gloss: Calmly, without excitement or disturbance.
examples: Cows grazed *placidly* in the field.
She smiled *placidly*, as if nothing had happened.
The lake lay *placidly* under the morning fog.

type: degree — informal, before a negative adjective
position: before its word — often after *just* (*just plain wrong*)
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *plain*
contrast: Informal and mostly American, usually with *just*: *just plain wrong*. Don't confuse it with the adjective *plain* (simple, without decoration: *a plain shirt*) or with *plainly* (clearly: *plainly visible*).

senses.gloss: Simply; completely — for emphasis.
examples: That's just *plain* wrong.
He's not shy; he's *plain* rude.
Some people are just *plain* lucky.

senses.gloss: Clearly; obviously.
examples: He was *plainly* upset about the news.
*Plainly*, something has to change.
The sign was *plainly* visible from the road.

senses.gloss: Directly and honestly, in simple words.
examples: Let me put it *plainly*: you're fired.
She spoke *plainly* about her illness.

senses.gloss: Simply, without decoration.
examples: The room was *plainly* furnished.
He was dressed *plainly* in jeans and a T-shirt.

senses.gloss: In a sad, high sound, as if asking for sympathy.
examples: The dog whined *plaintively* at the door.
"Can't we stay a little longer?" she asked *plaintively*.
A train whistle sounded *plaintively* in the distance.

senses.gloss: In a way that seems reasonable or likely to be true.
examples: He argued *plausibly* that the fire was an accident.
The story could *plausibly* be true.
She explained *plausibly* why she was late.

senses.gloss: In a fun, joking way, not seriously.
examples: She punched him *playfully* on the arm.
The puppies wrestled *playfully* on the rug.
"Maybe I will, maybe I won't," he said *playfully*.

senses.gloss: In a way that begs for something.
examples: The kids looked at their mom *pleadingly*.
"Please don't tell anyone," he said *pleadingly*.
The dog stared *pleadingly* at my sandwich.

modifies: adjectives and past participles (*pleasantly surprised*), verbs

senses.gloss: In a way that is enjoyable or nice.
examples: I was *pleasantly* surprised by how good the food was.
The evening was *pleasantly* cool.

senses.gloss: In a friendly, polite way.
examples: The receptionist smiled *pleasantly* and asked us to wait.
He greeted everyone *pleasantly* at the door.

position: any position — usually at the start or end of a request
modifies: requests, commands and replies to offers
contrast: Russian пожалуйста does jobs *please* can't. After *thank you*, say *You're welcome*, not *Please*. When handing something over, say *Here you go*. To accept an offer, say *Yes, please*. *Please* doesn't make a bare command fully polite: *Could you close the door, please?* is softer than *Close the door, please*. As a verb, *please* means радовать, угождать: *She's hard to please*.

senses.gloss: Used to make a request polite, or to accept an offer (*Yes, please*).
examples: Can I have a glass of water, *please*?
*Please* don't park in front of the garage.
"Would you like some coffee?" "Yes, *please*."

senses.gloss: In a way that gives pleasure or satisfaction.
examples: The design is simple and *pleasingly* modern.
The colors blend together *pleasingly*.
The novel is *pleasingly* short.

position: before its word — an adjective, often with *enough*
contrast: *Plenty* is usually a pronoun: *plenty of time* (много, достаточно времени). The adverb, straight before an adjective, is informal American: *It's plenty warm*, never *plenty of warm*. In formal writing use *quite* or *more than*: *more than big enough*.

senses.gloss: Very or more than enough — informal.
examples: The room is *plenty* big enough for two beds.
It's *plenty* warm in here, so turn off the heater.
Trust me, he's *plenty* smart.

position: end — or front and between commas for the fitting sense

senses.gloss: In a beautiful, expressive way, like poetry.
examples: She writes *poetically* about the desert.
He described their first meeting *poetically*.

senses.gloss: Fittingly, in a way so neat it seems planned, as in a story.
examples: The sun set, *poetically*, just as the song ended.
*Poetically*, he hit a home run in the last game before he retired.

position: mid or end — or before an adjective

senses.gloss: In a way that makes you feel sad or deeply moved.
examples: The film *poignantly* captures the pain of losing a parent.
Her letter was *poignantly* simple.
The song ends *poignantly* with a single piano note.
